title: Algebraically closed scalar extension of finite-group representation rings
statement:
Let $k,L$ be algebraically closed fields of characteristic zero [def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $\iota:k\hookrightarrow L$ be a field homomorphism, and let $G$ be finite. A representation is a finite-dimensional vector space with a linear group action. Define $R_k(G)$ and $R_L(G)$ as the abelian groups on representation isomorphism classes modulo $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$, with multiplication induced by diagonal tensor product. Scalar extension $V\mapsto L\otimes_{k,\iota}V$, with $g(a\otimes v)=a\otimes gv$, induces a ring isomorphism
$$b_{\iota,G}:R_k(G)\xrightarrow{\sim}R_L(G).$$
Scalar extension preserves dimension and induces a bijection on the isomorphism classes of irreducible representations. For every subgroup $H\leq G$, composition with $\iota$ induces a bijection $\operatorname{Hom}(H,k^\times)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}(H,L^\times)$. It commutes with induction and restriction, in particular
$$b_{\iota,G}([\operatorname{Ind}_H^G k_\lambda])=[\operatorname{Ind}_H^G L_{\iota\lambda}].$$
Here $k_\lambda$ is the line with $h\cdot a=\lambda(h)a$; for either coefficient field $A$, $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W$ means the quotient of $A[G]\otimes_A W$ by $[gh]\otimes w=[g]\otimes hw$ with action by left translation. Finally, if $A$ is any fixed algebraic closure of $\mathbf Q$ and $L$ is any algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, an embedding $A\hookrightarrow L$ extending the prime-field embedding exists.

proof.text: Write $V_L=L\otimes_{k,\iota}V$ and $B=k[G]$. A representation is a $B$-module via $(\sum c_g[g])v=\sum c_g(gv)$; the two actions recover each other on $[g]$. The $[g]$ form a finite basis, so $B$ is finite-dimensional. There is an $L$-algebra isomorphism $L\otimes_kB\simeq L[G]$ given by $a\otimes\sum c_g[g]\mapsto\sum a\iota(c_g)[g]$, with inverse $\sum a_g[g]\mapsto\sum a_g\otimes[g]$; multiplication agrees on basis elements. For a $k$-basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $V$, the maps $L^n\to V_L$, $(a_j)\mapsto\sum a_j\otimes v_j$, and $a\otimes\sum c_jv_j\mapsto(a\iota(c_j))_j$ are inverses by the tensor relations. Thus $\dim_LV_L=\dim_kV$, including zero.

proof.text: Let $S$ be irreducible over $k$. Schur's scalar-endomorphism theorem applied to $B$ and $S$ gives $\operatorname{End}_B(S)=k$. Its hypotheses hold: $k$ is algebraically closed and $S$ is nonzero, finite-dimensional, and simple as a $B$-module. The Hom scalar-extension theorem, using the algebra identification in Step 1, therefore identifies $\operatorname{End}_{L[G]}(S_L)$ with $L\otimes_k k=L$ as an algebra, with scalars acting as scalars. The dimension calculation makes $S_L$ nonzero. Apply finite-group semisimple decomposition over $L$. If the resulting direct sum had at least two nonzero summands, projection onto the first would be an equivariant idempotent different from both zero and the identity. In the field $L$, an idempotent $c$ satisfies $c(c-1)=0$, hence is zero or one. Thus the decomposition has exactly one summand, proving that $S_L$ is irreducible.

proof.text: For simple $k$-representations $S,T$, every nonzero equivariant map $S\to T$ is an isomorphism: its kernel is a proper stable subspace of $S$, hence zero, and its nonzero stable image is all of $T$. In particular, if $S$ and $T$ are not isomorphic then $\operatorname{Hom}_{k[G]}(S,T)=0$. The Hom scalar-extension theorem makes $\operatorname{Hom}_{L[G]}(S_L,T_L)=0$ in that case. Consequently $S_L$ and $T_L$ cannot be isomorphic. This proves injectivity on simple isomorphism classes; all modules and $k[G]$ satisfy the finite-dimensional hypotheses of that theorem.

proof.text: Decompose the regular $k$-representation $k[G]$ into finitely many simple representations $S_1,\ldots,S_r$ using finite-group semisimple decomposition. The tensor relations identify extension of this finite direct sum with $\bigoplus_j(S_j)_L$, using $a\otimes(v_j)_j\mapsto(a\otimes v_j)_j$ and the sum of the summand inclusions for its inverse. Hence Step 1 gives $L[G]\simeq\bigoplus_j(S_j)_L$. For any irreducible $L$-representation $W$, choose $0\ne w\in W$. The $L[G]$-linear map $L[G]\to W$, $\sum a_g[g]\mapsto\sum a_g(gw)$, is nonzero because it sends $[1]$ to $w$. One of its restrictions to the displayed summands is nonzero. That summand is simple by Step 2, so the kernel-and-image argument of Step 3 makes the restriction an isomorphism onto $W$. Thus every irreducible over $L$ occurs as an extension from $k$.

proof.text: For either field $F=k,L$, semisimple decomposition writes every finite-dimensional representation as a finite sum of simple ones. The multiplicity of a fixed simple $T$ is determined by $\dim_F\operatorname{Hom}_{F[G]}(T,V)$: Hom into a finite sum is the sum of the Hom spaces by taking components; a nonzero map between simples is an isomorphism by the kernel-and-image argument; Schur's theorem gives dimension one for $\operatorname{End}_{F[G]}(T)$. Consequently the direct-sum monoid of representation classes is the free commutative monoid on simple classes, and imposing $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ gives the free abelian group on those classes (the multiplicity maps are inverse to the generator map). Steps 2--4 give a bijection of those bases, so scalar extension induces an additive isomorphism $b_{\iota,G}$.

proof.text:
The tensor relations define inverse equivariant $L$-linear maps
$$V_L\otimes_L W_L\ \rightleftarrows\ (V\otimes_kW)_L,\qquad (a\otimes v)\otimes(b\otimes w)\mapsto ab\otimes(v\otimes w),\quad c\otimes(v\otimes w)\mapsto(c\otimes v)\otimes(1\otimes w).$$
For example, the $L$-balancing relation moves $b$ to the first factor, giving the first inverse identity; the $k$-balancing relation moves $\iota(t)$ to the coefficient for $t\in k$, giving the other relations. Diagonal action agrees on the generators. The unit comparison is $L\otimes_k k\to L$, $a\otimes c\mapsto a\iota(c)$, with inverse $a\mapsto a\otimes1$. Thus $b_{\iota,G}$ preserves products and the unit, making the additive isomorphism a ring isomorphism. Restriction to $H\le G$ has the identical vector space and $H$-action on both sides, so commutes with scalar extension. Dimension preservation was proved in Step 1.

proof.text: For any homomorphism $\mu:H\to L^\times$ and $h\in H$, finiteness makes two powers among $1,h,\ldots,h^{|H|}$ equal, so $h^n=1$ for some $n>0$ and $\mu(h)^n=1$. Over the algebraically closed field $k$, repeatedly finding a root of a nonconstant polynomial and dividing by the corresponding linear factor writes $X^n-1=\prod_{j=1}^n(X-c_j)$ with $c_j\in k$. Applying $\iota$ and evaluating at $\mu(h)$ shows that some $\mu(h)-\iota(c_j)$ is zero, since a field has no zero divisors. Thus $\mu(h)$ lies in $\iota(k^\times)$. Its unique preimages $\lambda(h)$ satisfy $\lambda(hh')=\lambda(h)\lambda(h')$ and $\lambda(1)=1$ by injectivity of $\iota$. This gives the inverse to composition with $\iota$ on character homomorphisms. The line comparison $L\otimes_k k_\lambda\simeq L_{\iota\lambda}$ is $a\otimes c\mapsto a\iota(c)$: applying $h$ multiplies its value by $\iota(\lambda(h))$.

proof.text:
Let $W$ be any finite-dimensional $k$-representation of $H$. On the induced quotients defined in the statement, define
$$L\otimes_k\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W\ \rightleftarrows\ \operatorname{Ind}_H^G(W_L),\qquad a\otimes([g]\otimes w)\mapsto[g]\otimes(a\otimes w),\quad [g]\otimes(a\otimes w)\mapsto a\otimes([g]\otimes w).$$
Both formulas respect addition and $k$-balancing; $L$-linearity moves a coefficient on $[g]$ into the $L$-coefficient $a$. The subgroup relation on either side maps to the same equality $[gh]\otimes(a\otimes w)=[g]\otimes(a\otimes hw)$, because $h$ fixes $a$. Hence the maps descend and are inverse on all generators. Left translation on $[g]$ commutes with both formulas, so they are equivariant. Choosing representatives $t$ for the cosets $tH$ and writing $g=th$ identifies either induced quotient with a finite direct sum of copies of $W$ (or $W_L$); the inverse sends $[th]\otimes w$ to $hw$ in the $t$-coordinate. Thus these are finite-dimensional representations. Together with Step 7 this proves the displayed induction formula, and proves commutation with induction for arbitrary representations and their classes.

proof.text: Give $L$ its $\mathbf Q$-algebra structure by the unique prime-field embedding, which exists since $\operatorname{char}L=0$. The fixed algebraic closure $A$ is algebraic over $\mathbf Q$ by definition. Apply the algebraic-extension embedding theorem to $K=\mathbf Q$, the extension $A/K$, the algebraically closed target $L$, and the prime-field map. It supplies a field homomorphism $A\to L$ extending that map. A unital homomorphism of fields is injective (its kernel is an ideal other than the whole field), giving the required embedding.
